extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, students and researchers seeking a comparative overview of defamation law
extracted.subtask_description: A country-by-country summary of legal definitions, offences, defenses, penalties, and procedural rules relating to defamation (libel, slander, insult), including civil and criminal forms and online/cyber variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: General definition of defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined as "the allegation or [the] allocation of a fact that damages the honor or reputation of the person or body to which the fact is imputed". A defamatory allegation is considered an insult if it does not include any facts or if the claimed facts cannot be verified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the baseline distinction between defamatory allegations (factual imputations) and insults (no factual content or unverifiable facts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Germany — unified libel/slander rules and Criminal Code sections
rubrics_metrics.description: In German law, there is no distinction between libel and slander. Relevant offences in the Criminal Code include §90 (denigration of the Federal President), §90a (denigration of the State and its symbols), §90b (unconstitutional denigration of the organs of the Constitution), §185 ("insult"), §186 (defamation of character), §187 (defamation with deliberate untruths), §188 (political defamation with increased penalties for offending against paras 186 and 187), §189 (denigration of a deceased person), §192 ("insult" with true statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also lists related procedural sections (§190–§200) covering proof, exceptions (no defamation in pursuit of rightful interests), criminal prosecution application, mutual insult, and methods of proclamation; notes rising defamation lawsuits as of 2006.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greece — penalties and statute highlights
rubrics_metrics.description: Maximum prison term for defamation, libel or insult was five years, while the maximum fine was €15,000. Crime of insult (Article 361) could lead to up to one year imprisonment or a fine; unprovoked insult punished with at least three months. Defamation up to two months or a fine; aggravated defamation at least three months plus possible fine and deprivation of civil rights; disparaging memory of deceased punished with up to six months imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes statutory penalties and distinctions among insult, unprovoked insult, aggravated defamation, and offences affecting civil rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: India — criminal and civil options; constitutional limits and IPC sections
rubrics_metrics.description: A defamation case can be filed under either criminal law or civil law, or both. Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech) is subject to "reasonable restrictions" including defamation. Section 499 of the IPC (now replaced by Section 356 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) defines defamation and lists ten exceptions. Punishment (Section 500) is simple imprisonment up to two years, or a fine, or both. Other related offences include false statements regarding elections (Sec 171G), false information (Sec 182), false claims in court (Sec 209), false criminal charges (Sec 211), and various insult-related sections (e.g., 295A, 298, 504, 509).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under CrPC, defamation is prosecuted only upon complaint (within six months) and is bailable, non-cognisable and compoundable. The entry emphasizes constitutional tension between free speech and reasonable restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ireland — Defamation Act 2009 changes and statute of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The revised Defamation Act 2009 repealed older statutes and represented significant changes, shifting weight toward media freedom. Statute of limitations is one year from first publication (may be extended to two years by courts) (Section 38).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that the 2009 Act aimed to correct perceived previous over-emphasis on individual reputation versus media freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Israel — civil and criminal defamation; remedies and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Defamation Prohibition Law (1965), defamation can be either civil or criminal. As a civil offence, courts may award compensation up to NIS 50,000 without plaintiff proving material damage. As a criminal offence, defamation is punishable by a year of imprisonment; to be a felony it must be intentional and target at least two persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes compensation regime in tort from criminal elements and thresholds for felony treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italy — injury and defamation crimes, penalties and professional bans
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime of injury (Article 594) offended someone's honour in their presence (up to six months prison or fine); crime of defamation (Article 595) refers to offending reputation before many persons (up to one year prison or fine; doubled if attribution of a determined fact). Offences via press or publicity carry higher penalties (six months to three years or fines). From 15 January 2016, injury became a tort (not a crime) while defamation remained a crime. Article 31 adds temporary bans for crimes committed with abuse of power or profession, meaning journalists convicted of libel may be banned from the profession. False accusations may trigger calunnia (Article 368).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains differentiation by medium and nature of allegation, and special sanctions for abuse of profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Japan — civil remedies and Penal Code provisions (defamation and insults)
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil: under article 723 of the Civil Code, courts can order tortfeasors to take suitable measures to restore reputation and/or award compensation. Criminal: Penal Code articles include Article 230/230-2 (Defamation), Article 231 (Insults), with a special provision allowing proof of truth as a defence for matters concerning public interest; some offences prosecuted only upon complaint. Other related offences: damage to foreign flags (Art 92), false accusations (Art 172), desecrating places of worship (Art 188), and damage to credibility/obstruction of business (Art 233).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes constitutional protection of expression (Art 21) and example cases where courts balanced constitutional grounds against procedural errors; highlights that veracity may not determine guilt unless public interest provision applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malaysia — tort and criminal offence with reliance on case law
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation is both a tort and a criminal offence; principal statutes are Defamation Act 1957 (Revised 1983) and the Penal Code. Malaysian law follows common law jurisdictions (UK, Singapore, India) and relies on case law; the Defamation Act 1957 is similar to English Defamation Act 1952.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes statutory and case-law mixture and comparative statutory origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mexico — abolition in federal code and state variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Crimes of calumny, defamation and slanderous allegation (injurias) have been abolished in the Federal Penal Code and in fifteen states; they remain in the penal codes of seventeen states with average prison penalties from 1.1 to 3.8 years depending on conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights federal decriminalization trend and uneven state-level retention with variable penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Netherlands — civil remedies and correction/injunction powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation is mostly addressed by civil complaint at District Court. Article 167 of Book 6 Civil Code: when someone is liable for incorrect or misleading publication of factual information, the court may order the tortfeasor to publish a correction in a way set by the court; injunctions often require deletion or publication of a rectification statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on civil court ordering corrective measures and deletions or rectifications rather than criminal penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norway — historical criminal penalties and decriminalization shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Previously a crime punishable with up to six months or fine, with higher penalties for harm to 'good name' up to one year and up to two years if in print/broadcast or aggravating circumstances; acting 'against his better judgment' could lead to three years. Under a new Penal Code decided in 2005, defamation would cease to be a crime; Criminal Code took effect on 1 October 2015 moving defamation to civil law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes transition from criminal to civil treatment and explains prosecution initiation rules (offended person must initiate unless directed to an indefinite group).

rubrics_metrics.name: Philippines — Revised Penal Code definitions, presumed malice, and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: ARTICLE 353 defines libel as a public and malicious imputation of a crime or vice tending to cause dishonor or contempt. Malice is presumed even if true; exceptions include private communications in course of duty and fair reports without comments. Punishment for libel in writing/similar mediums includes imprisonment, fine, civil action (Art. 355). Other articles address threats to publish libel for extortion, private-life facts in press, slander (oral), slander by deed, responsibility for dissemination, and conditions for defence of truth (good motives, justifiable ends) — truth defence limited for non-criminal activities unless related to official duties (Art. 361). Statute of limitations varies (two years for libel, six months for slander, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes real-world cases (e.g., broadcaster jailed) and UN Human Rights Committee involvement questioning compatibility with freedom of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philippines (online) — Cybercrime Prevention Act and electronic libel
rubrics_metrics.description: Republic Act 10175 (Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012) provides that libel committed through a computer system (electronic libel) is criminally punishable; electronic libel punished with imprisonment from six years and one day up to twelve years (per commentary). Multiple petitions challenging constitutionality were filed alleging infringements on freedom of expression, due process, equal protection, and privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights legal and constitutional controversies and ongoing court challenges; notes the interplay with high-profile cases (e.g., Rappler).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poland — public-accusation standard and media aggravation
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation is a crime consisting of accusing someone of conduct that may degrade them in public opinion or expose them to loss of confidence necessary for a position; penalties include fine, limitation of liberty and imprisonment up to one year (Article 212.1). Penalty is more severe when offence happens through the media (Article 212.2). Public insults against protected characteristics can carry up to three years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the role of public dissemination and aggravation when media or protected-class insults are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portugal — categories of defamation crimes and aggravated penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Crimes: 'defamation' (art. 180; up to six months prison or fine), 'injuries' (art. 181; up to three months or fine), 'offence to the memory of a deceased person' (art.185; up to six months or fine). Penalties aggravated with publicity (art.183; up to two years or at least 120 days fine) and when victim is an authority (art.184; penalties increased by half); extra penalty of public knowledge of court decision and publication costs (art.189) and 'incitement of a crime' (art.297; up to three years or fine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains aggravating factors (publicity, authority-targeted) and remedies including publication of decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romania — decriminalization of defamation since 2014
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2014, defamation is no longer criminalized in the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates legislative/decriminalization trend in this jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saudi Arabia — defamation of the state or rulers under terrorism laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation of the state, or a past or present ruler, is punishable under terrorism legislation. Example: under a 2014 counterterrorism law, actions that 'threaten Saudi Arabia's unity, disturb public order, or defame the reputation of the state or the king' are considered acts of terrorism; suspects can be held incommunicado for 90 days without a lawyer during initial questioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights severity and use of counterterrorism statutes to address reputational attacks on state/royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singapore — Protection from Harassment Act remedies and distinct scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Division 2 of Part 3 of the Protection from Harassment Act 2014 provides for Stop Publication Orders, Correction Orders, and Disabling Orders requiring intermediaries to disable access. This is distinct from common law libel/slander and the Defamation Act 1957. The Act addresses conduct that causes 'harassment, alarm, or distress' and is designed to avoid outlawing an overly broad range of speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes availability of non-traditional remedies (disabling orders for intermediaries) and narrower scope to avoid overbroad speech restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: South Africa — reference to crimen injuria
rubrics_metrics.description: Main article: Crimen injuria (not expanded in this chunk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals that South Africa addresses reputation via crimen injuria (offensive conduct harming dignity/reputation); full criteria are in main article.

rubrics_metrics.name: South Korea — criminal and civil liability, truth/public interest defence, and online impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Both true and false statements can be considered defamation; penalties increase for false statements. A person can be criminally defamed posthumously. Criminal defamation occurs when a public statement damages the subject's reputation unless the statement was true and presented solely for the public interest. Criminal law allows imprisonment (up to seven years for false allegations) and fines; civil damages also possible. Police act as judicial investigators and criminal actions generally proceed civil ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes examples of online celebrity attacks linked to suicides and the rise of cyber defamation complaints; mentions legislative proposals to allow up to three years imprisonment for online defamation and police investigative powers without prior complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: South Korea (online) — cyber defamation and game-related insults
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported increases in online attacks and cyber defamation cases (numbers cited for 2010, 2014, 2015). Many complaints were game-related and often involved teenagers; settlement fees ranged from 300,000 to 2,000,000 won. Courts have approved arrests in high-profile online misinformation cases affecting national credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates societal impact, settlement-money hunting phenomenon, and statistic-backed growth in cyber-insult complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Former Soviet Union — defamatory insults as criminal offences only
rubrics_metrics.description: In the former Soviet Union, defamatory insults can only constitute a criminal offence, not a civil wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with jurisdictions where defamation is primarily a civil tort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spain — calumny (calumnia) vs injury (injuria) and publication penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Calumny (Article 205) is accusing someone of a crime knowing it is false or with reckless contempt for truth; penalties for publicity cases are imprisonment six months to two years or fine of 12–24 months-fine; for other cases only a fine. Injury (Article 208) consists of hurting dignity or reputation and applies if the offence is strong; penalties are fines (three–seven months or six–fourteen months if strong and with publicity). Article 216 allows judges to order publication of judicial decision at the defamer's expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes mens rea (knowledge of falsity) for calumny and public-impact aggravations and judicial remedies for publication of decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweden — denigration, gross defamation, insulting behaviour, and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Denigration (ärekränkning) criminalized by Chapter 5 of the Criminal Code. Article 1 (defamation/förtal): pointing someone out as a criminal or 'having a reprehensible way of living' or providing vilifying information can be fined. Article 2 (gross defamation/grovt förtal): penalty up to two years or fine; courts consider content and scope of dissemination, and knowingly conveyed untruths. Article 4 criminalizes defaming deceased. Article 3 covers insulting behaviour (förolämpning), punishable with fine or up to six months if gross. Under press freedom exemptions both criminal and civil lawsuits may be brought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that statements need not be untrue to be punishable if intended to vilify; grossness depends on content and dissemination scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Switzerland — wilful defamation vs defamation and penalties/statute of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilful defamation punished with a maximum of three years in prison or a fine of at least thirty days' worth (Article 174-2). Wilful defamation requires knowledge of falsity and intent to ruin reputation (Articles 174-1 and 174-2). Ordinary defamation punished with a maximum monetary penalty of 180 daily penalty units (Article 173-1). For deceased or absent persons, statute of limitations is 30 years after death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes intent-based (wilful) offences from lesser monetary-penalty offences and notes long statute of limitations for claims against deceased/absent persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taiwan — civil and criminal code provisions and Constitutional Court interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil: Civil Code articles allow prevention, removal, and damages for emotional distress, compensation even if loss not purely pecuniary, measures to restore reputation, and statutes of limitations (two years after injury/tortfeasor known; otherwise ten years). Criminal: Criminal Code Chapter 27 lists insults (Art.309), slander/libel with harsher punishment for libel and truth as a defence except for private matters (Art.310), defences related to protection of legal interests/reports on public matters/fair comments (Art.311), insults of deceased (Art.312), damage to credibility with increased penalties via media/Internet (Art.313), and offences prosecuted only upon complaint (Art.314). Constitutional Court rulings (e.g., J.Y. Interpretation No. 509) have upheld constitutionality while requiring proportionality and elaborated standards for checking validity of defamatory statements about public matters (objective and reasonable grounds; actual malice standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the court's balancing of free speech and reputation, burden of proof for actual malice placed on prosecutor/accuser, and expectation of higher fact-checking by media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thailand — civil compensation standard and criminal code sections 326–327
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil & Commercial Code: person who asserts or circulates untruth injurious to reputation shall compensate for damage even if unaware of untruth if they ought to have known; exceptions when sender or receiver has rightful interest. Criminal Code Section 326 defines defamation (imputing to another before a third person in manner likely to impair reputation) punishable with up to one year imprisonment or fine up to 20,000 Baht or both. Section 327 penalizes defamation of the family of a deceased. Criminal defamation charges frequently used to censor journalists/activists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows civil strictness (liability even for unknown untruth if ought to have known) and common use of criminal charges for suppression of criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: United Kingdom — abolition of criminal libel and truth/public benefit in defence
rubrics_metrics.description: United Kingdom abolished criminal libel on 12 January 2010 by section 73 of the Coroners and Justice Act 2009. Under English common law historically, truth was a defence only in civil libel; criminal libel focused on breach of the peace. Section 6 of the Libel Act 1843 allowed proven truth as a defence in criminal libel if publication was for the 'public benefit'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes shift away from criminal treatment and emphasizes public-benefit requirement historically tied to truth defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States — rarity of criminal defamation and First Amendment constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Fewer than half of U.S. states have criminal defamation laws, and applicability is limited by the First Amendment; such laws are rarely enforced. No criminal defamation laws at federal level. Lists 23 states and two territories with criminal defamation statutes; Iowa criminalizes through case law. Notes that truth is generally a defence but case law nuances exist (e.g., Noonan v. Staples often misinterpreted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights constitutional limits (First Amendment), legislation addressing enforcement of offshore libel judgments (SPEECH Act) and anti-SLAPP concerns; references federal/state acts protecting writers from enforcement of foreign libel judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venezuela — example of civil action leading to imprisonment
rubrics_metrics.description: In March 2016, a civil action for defamation led to imposition of a four-year prison sentence on a newspaper publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an example of harsh criminal/custodial consequences following civil action in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yemen — online defamation campaign example
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2024 a judge and member of the Supreme Judicial Council, Sabah al-Alwani, was the subject of an online defamation campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates contemporary online defamation incidents involving public figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: UNESCO/Global statistics on criminalization
rubrics_metrics.description: As of 2012, defamation, slander, insult and lese-majesty laws existed across the world. According to ARTICLE 19, 174 countries retained criminal penalties for defamation, with full decriminalization in 21 countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides global context: widespread retention of criminal penalties and limited full decriminalization as of cited date.
